title: Huoshu: The Chinese Fire Rat and Fire-Washed Cloth
metaDescription: Huoshu means fire rat. Chinese literary accounts connect an animal living in fire with cloth made from its hair that is cleaned by burning.
description: Huoshu means fire rat. Chinese literary accounts connect an animal living in fire with cloth made from its hair that is cleaned by burning.
storyHooks: A ruler demands an indestructible robe. The tailor must decide whether to reveal that the treasured cloth protects its wearer but preserves every stain of guilt.

sections.origin: The fire-rat motif appears in Chinese descriptions of extraordinary places and materials. A passage collected in Gujin Tushu Jicheng quotes earlier material about a fiery mountain, fire animals, and cloth made from their hair.
sections.legend: The striking idea is fire-washed cloth: dirt disappears in the fire while the fabric survives. The animal supplies a story explaining a marvellous material, rather than a modern zoological description.
sections.variants: The compilation preserves differing descriptions of size, colour, and hair. Keep the quoted source attached to each detail instead of merging them into a single creature design. Similar cloth motifs need not describe the same animal.
sections.culture: For an adaptation, the material can drive the conflict. A garment that survives fire might expose a fraudulent gift or become evidence in a trial. Those plots are new uses of the motif, not recovered episodes from the cited text.

researchNote: The anthology transcription and indexed Qidong Yeyu passage were consulted. Their marvels are literary claims, not instructions for identifying real animals or testing fabrics.

questions.question: What is Huoshu in English?
questions.answer: Fire rat is a direct rendering of 火鼠.

questions.question: Does the text prove a real fireproof animal existed?
questions.answer: No. It records a literary explanation for a marvellous material, not biological verification.
